extracted.intended_audience: prokaryote taxonomists, microbiologists, and authors preparing new taxon names or changes for publication
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and recommendations governing valid publication, citation, orthography, and changes of names for prokaryotic taxa (species, subspecies, genera, higher taxa), including requirements for authorship citation, new combinations, conservation, rejection, and orthographic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation 30 – minimal standards before publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Before publication of the name and description of a new species, the examination and description should conform at least to the minimal standards (if available) required for the relevant taxon of prokaryote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists of minimal standards are being prepared for each group of prokaryotes (tests for establishment of generic identity and diagnosis of the species). Aim is to provide guidance without contradicting Principle 1(4). Exceptions considered by ICSP/Judicial Commission; see Appendix 6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 31a – ambiguous descriptions invalidate publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The name of a species or a subspecies is not validly published if the description is demonstrably ambiguous and cannot be critically identified for purposes of the precise application of the name of a taxon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given (e.g., ‘Methanobacillus omelianskii’ treated as illegitimate when description included all component species). If description applies to a single member it may be legitimate (example Syntrophobacter wolinii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 31b – consortium names not regulated
rubrics_metrics.description: The name of a consortium is not regulated by this Code, and such a name has no standing in nomenclature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition: a consortium is an aggregate or association of two or more organisms. Example: Cylindrogloea bacterifera Perfiliev 1914.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 32a – conditions for valid publication of a subspecies name
rubrics_metrics.description: For the name of a subspecies to be validly published, it must: (1) be published in conformity with Rules 27 and 28b; (2) be published as a ternary combination: generic name + specific epithet + subspecific epithet with abbreviation 'subsp.' between epithets; (3) author must clearly indicate that a subspecies is being named.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bacillus subtilis subsp. subtilis. See Rule 13a for rank abbreviation usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation 32a – apply species recommendations to subspecies
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations 30a and 30b apply to the name of a subspecies with replacement of the word 'species' by the word 'subspecies'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 32b – specific epithet unaffected by illegitimate generic name
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific (or subspecific) epithet is not rendered illegitimate by publication in a species (or subspecies) name in which the generic name is illegitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Chapter 3, Section 8, and example for Rule 20f. The epithet can be used in other combinations subject to rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 33a – indicate proposals for new taxa with abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: An author should indicate that a name is being proposed for a new taxon by the addition of the appropriate abbreviation for the category to which the taxon belongs (e.g., 'ord. nov.', 'gen. nov.', 'sp. nov.', 'comb. nov.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: Such abbreviations are often printed in Roman or boldface when following a Latin scientific name to differentiate them from the name. Examples: Actinomycetales ord. nov.; Actinomyces bovis sp. nov.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 33b – citation of previously proposed names must include author(s) and year
rubrics_metrics.description: The citation of the name of a taxon that has been previously proposed should include both the name of the author(s) who first published the name and the year of publication; for more than two authors use first author followed by 'et al.' and the year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Actinomyces bovis Harz 1877; Acetobacterium woodii Balch et al. 1977. Note: correct citation enables verification of date and original description; include page numbers of main text, not summary/abstract. Examples illustrating Approved Lists citation variants and use of 'nom. approb.' are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 33c – revival (nom. rev.) and attribution of pre-1980 names
rubrics_metrics.description: If a name or epithet published prior to 1 Jan 1980 but not included in an Approved List is proposed for a taxon, it must be attributed to the author of the proposal and cited according to Rules 33a, 33b, 34a and 34b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes: indicate 'nom. rev.' for revived names; to show original authors add 'ex' and original author/year in parentheses followed by 'nom. rev.' Examples provided; use 'non' to indicate revived name used for a different taxon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 34a – indicate formation of a new combination (comb. nov.)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an author transfers a species to another genus, or a subspecies to another species, the author should indicate the formation of the new combination by adding the abbreviation 'comb. nov.'; use 'nom. nov.' when a new specific epithet is substituted due to homonymy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used when retaining original specific epithet; the original name is called the basonym. Example: Anaerovibrio glycerini → Anaerosinus glycerini (Schauder and Schink 1996) Strömpl et al. 1999.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 34b – citation format for new combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The citation of a new combination previously proposed should include the name of the original author in parentheses followed by the name(s) of the author(s) who proposed the new combination and the year of publication of the new combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer inclusion of the date of the original author's publication. If author who formed the new combination substituted a new specific epithet to avoid homonymy, the name of the author of the original specific epithet is omitted. Examples: Microbacterium oxydans (Chatelain and Second 1966) Schumann et al. 1999; Flavobacterium hydatis Bernardet et al. 1996 (original author omitted in that case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 34c – citation when rank altered but name retained
rubrics_metrics.description: When a taxon from subspecies to genus is altered in rank but retains its name or epithet, the original author(s) must be cited in parentheses followed by the author(s) who effected the alteration and the year of publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided showing conversion between genus and subspecies with correct citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 35 – citation when circumscription emended (emend.)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an alteration of the diagnostic characters or of the circumscription of a taxon modifies the nature of the taxon, the author responsible may be indicated by adding 'emend.' followed by the name of the author responsible for the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Rhodopseudomonas Czurda and Maresch 1937 emend. van Niel 1944.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 36 – citation for name conserved so as to exclude the type
rubrics_metrics.description: A name conserved so as to exclude the type is not to be ascribed to the original author; the author whose concept of the name is conserved must be cited as authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Aeromonas attributed to Stanier 1943 (with new type species) rather than to original authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 37a – change of name when nomenclatural type excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: The name of a taxon must be changed if the nomenclatural type of the taxon is excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retention of a name that excludes the type can only be effected by conservation by the Judicial Commission, who establishes a new type upon conservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 37b – permissible reasons for name change
rubrics_metrics.description: A change in the name of a taxon is not warranted by alteration of diagnostic characters or circumscription; a change may be required by: (1) an Opinion of the Judicial Commission; (2) transfer of the taxon; (3) union with another taxon; (4) change of its rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 38 – priority when uniting taxa of same rank
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more taxa of the same rank are united, the name of the taxon under which they are united is chosen by the rule of priority of publication (oldest legitimate name retained).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If this choice would lead to confusion in bacteriology, the author should refer the matter to the Judicial Commission. Example: retention of Salmonella over Eberthella.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 39a – division of a genus: retention of generic name
rubrics_metrics.description: If a genus is divided into two or more genera or subgenera, the generic name must be retained for one of these (the one including the type). If not retained previously, it must be reestablished under Rule 39b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if Bacillus divided into Bacillus and Aerobacillus, the subgenus including type species Bacillus subtilis must be named Bacillus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 39b – when a type has been designated, name retention
rubrics_metrics.description: When a particular species has been designated as the type, the generic name must be retained for the genus which includes that species; when no type was designated a type must be chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial note that future need for this may be reduced; see Rule 27.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 39c – principles apply to subgenera divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The principles of Rules 39a and 39b apply when a subgenus is divided into two or more subgenera: the original subgeneric name retained for the subgenus containing the type species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 40a – division of a species preserves original specific epithet for one resultant taxon
rubrics_metrics.description: When a species is divided into two or more species or subspecies, the specific epithet of the original species must be retained for one of the taxa into which the species is divided or reestablished if not retained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Rule 50a when a subspecies is elevated to species. Example discussed regarding Bacillus/Paenibacillus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 40b – retention of specific epithet for taxon including the type strain
rubrics_metrics.description: The specific epithet must be retained for the species or subspecies which includes the type strain. When no type was designated, one must be chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if Bacillus subtilis divided into subspecies, the subspecies containing the type strain must be named Bacillus subtilis subsp. subtilis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 40c – principles for subspecies division
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles of Rules 40a and 40b apply when a subspecies is divided into two or more subspecies: original subspecies name retained for the subspecies containing the type strain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: identical specific and subspecific epithets in a type subspecies do not contravene Rule 12b because they are based on same type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 40d – automatic creation of type subspecies when a subspecific name excludes the type
rubrics_metrics.description: Valid publication of a subspecific name which excludes the type of the species automatically creates another subspecies which includes the type and whose name bears the same specific and subspecific epithets as the name of the type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Publication of Bacillus subtilis subsp. spizizenii automatically created Bacillus subtilis subsp. subtilis. The author of the species name is cited as author of the automatically created subspecific name; examples provided showing correct authorship citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 41a – transfer of species to another genus retains specific epithet except in two cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When a species is transferred to another genus without change of rank, the specific epithet must be retained (or reestablished) unless: (1) the resulting binary combination would be a later homonym; (2) there is available an earlier validly published and legitimate specific or subspecific epithet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of homonym case: Flavobacterium hydatis proposed for Cytophaga aquatilis because Flavobacterium aquatile already existed in that genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 41b – when generic name changed, specific epithets retained
rubrics_metrics.description: When the name of a genus is changed, the specific epithets of the species included under the original generic name must be retained for the same species if they are transferred to the new genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 42 – union of taxa of equal rank uses oldest legitimate name; tie-breaker
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more taxa of the same rank are united, the oldest legitimate name or epithet is retained. If names/epithets are of same date, the author who first unites the taxa has the right to choose one of them and that choice must be followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation 42 gives practical preferences when choosing between two generic names of the same date: (1) prefer better known; (2) prefer one first accompanied by description of a species; (3) if both accompanied by descriptions, prefer one including larger number of species; (4) if equal, prefer the more appropriate name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 43 – union of genera as subgenera naming
rubrics_metrics.description: When several genera are united as subgenera of one genus, the subgenus which includes the type species of the genus under which union takes place must bear the same name as that genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: subgenus containing type species Lactobacillus delbrueckii must be named Lactobacillus, not Thermobacterium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 44 – union of species from different genera into a genus: name derived from earliest type species
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more species of different genera are brought together to form a genus, and these species include the type species of one or more genera, the name of the genus is that associated with the type species having the earliest legitimate generic name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no type species is placed in the genus, propose a new generic name and select a type species. Example: Brevibacterium proposed where none of included species was a type species of previous genera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 45 – union of several species as subspecies under one species
rubrics_metrics.description: When several species are united as subspecies under one species, the subspecies which includes the type strain of the species under whose name they are united must be designated by the same epithet as the species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Streptomyces griseus subsp. griseus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 46 – placeholder rule not to be cited
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial Note: former Rule 46 has been relocated as Rule 40d. This rule remains only as a placeholder to avoid renumbering Rules 47 and above and should not be cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 47a – union of taxa above species: derive higher taxon name from earliest legitimate type genus
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more taxa of the same rank from subtribe to family inclusive are united under a taxon of higher rank, the higher-ranking taxon should derive its name from the earliest legitimate genus that is a type genus of one of the lower-ranking taxa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using that generic name would lead to confusion, the author may choose as type a genus that leads to least confusion and should refer to Judicial Commission if in doubt. Note: the type of a taxon above genus is one of the contained genera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 47b – if no type genera placed, propose new name based on selected type
rubrics_metrics.description: If no type genera were placed in the taxon, a new name based on the selected type must be proposed for the taxon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided (Peptococcaceae Rogosa 1971).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 48 – change in rank between subgenus and order: retain stem, alter suffix
rubrics_metrics.description: When the rank of a taxon between subgenus and order is changed, the stem of the name must be retained and only the suffix altered unless the resulting name must be rejected under the Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Elevation of tribe Pseudomonadeae to family Pseudomonadaceae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 49 – lowering genus to subgenus or raising subgenus to genus retains original name
rubrics_metrics.description: When a genus is lowered in rank to subgenus, the original name must be retained unless rejected under the Rules. This also applies when a subgenus is elevated to a genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided showing correct citation when rank changes (e.g., Branhamella lowered to subgenus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 50a – elevation of subspecies to species uses subspecific epithet
rubrics_metrics.description: When a subspecies is elevated in rank to a species, the subspecific epithet in the name of the subspecies must be used as the specific epithet of the species name unless the resulting combination is illegitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Campylobacter pylori subsp. mustelae → Campylobacter mustelae (Fox et al. 1988) Fox et al. 1989.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 50b – lowering species to subspecies uses specific epithet as subspecific epithet
rubrics_metrics.description: When a species is lowered in rank to a subspecies, the specific epithet in the name of the species must be used as the subspecific epithet of the subspecies name unless the resulting combination is illegitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bifidobacterium globosum → Bifidobacterium pseudolongum subsp. globosum with correct citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 51a – illegitimate names contrary to Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A name contrary to a Rule is illegitimate and may not be used. However, a name illegitimate in one taxonomic position is not necessarily illegitimate in another position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Diplococcus illegitimate when combined with Streptococcus because not earlier name; legitimate when accepted as separate genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 51b – common reasons a name may be illegitimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasons include: (1) taxon circumscription included the nomenclatural type of a name which ought to have been adopted; (2) author failed to adopt earliest legitimate generic/specific/subspecific epithet available; (3) its specific epithet must be rejected under Rules 52 or 53; (4) it is a later homonym of a name of a taxon of prokaryotes, fungi, algae, protozoa, or viruses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided for each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 52 – words not regarded as specific or subspecific epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: The following are not to be regarded as specific or subspecific epithets: (1) a word or phrase not intended as specific epithet; (2) ordinal adjective higher than ten used for enumeration; (3) a number or letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Bacillus nova species' (not an epithet), ordinal adjectives (undecimus), and letters/numbers (α in Bacillus α von Freudenreich).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 53 – duplicate epithets illegitimate within same genus
rubrics_metrics.description: An epithet is illegitimate if it duplicates a specific or subspecific epithet previously validly published for a species or subspecies of the same genus but which is a different bacterium whose name is based upon another type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided (Corynebacterium helvolum cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 54 – replacement of illegitimate names and epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: A name or epithet illegitimate under Rules 51b, 53, or 56a is replaced by the oldest legitimate name or epithet in a binary or ternary combination which will accord with the Rules. If no legitimate name exists, one must be chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific epithet published under an illegitimate generic name may be used in another genus if no obstacle; resultant combination is treated as a new name ascribed to the author of the combination but epithet ascribed to original author. Example: Pfeifferella pseudomallei → Pseudomonas pseudomallei.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 55 – legitimate names are not to be replaced for listed subjective reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate name or epithet may not be replaced merely because it is: (1) inappropriate; (2) disagreeable; (3) another name is preferable; (4) another name is better known; (5) no longer describes the organism; (6) has been cited incorrectly (incorrect citation can be rectified by later author).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided for each reason (e.g., Bacteroides melaninogenicus, Miyagawanella lymphogranulomatis, Haemophilus influenzae).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 56a – rejection of names by Judicial Commission (nomina rejicienda)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the Judicial Commission can place names on the list of rejected names. A name may be placed on this list for reasons including: (1) ambiguous name (nomen ambiguum); (2) doubtful name (nomen dubium); (3) name causing confusion (nomen confusum); (4) perplexing name (nomen perplexum); (5) perilous name (nomen periculosum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and definitions given. Note 1 restricts application concerning changes in specific epithets of nomenspecies that are widely recognized as contagious/virulent; Commission may issue Opinion to maintain taxon separate for safety/economic reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 56b – conservation of names (nomina conservanda)
rubrics_metrics.description: A conserved name is a name which must be used instead of all earlier synonyms and homonyms; only the Judicial Commission can place names on the list of conserved names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: a conserved name is conserved against all other names for the taxon so long as the taxon is not united with another taxon bearing a legitimate name; upon union the earlier competing name is adopted according to priority rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 57a – orthography follows source spelling and Latin rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Any name or epithet should be written in conformity with the spelling of the word from which it is derived and in strict accordance with the rules of Latin and latinization. Exceptions provided for typographic/orthographic errors and orthographic variants (Rules 61, 62a, 62b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Appendix 9 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 57b – definition of orthographic variant
rubrics_metrics.description: In this Code, orthographic variant means a name (or epithet) differing only in transliteration into Latin of the same word from a language other than Latin or in its grammatical correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Haemophilus, Hemophilus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 57c – perplexing names treated and referred to Judicial Commission
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more generic names or two or more epithets in the same genus are so similar as to cause uncertainty they may be treated as perplexing names (nomina perplexa) and the matter referred to the Judicial Commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given (Bacillus limnophilus vs Bacillus limophilus). Note 1: orthographic variants may be corrected by any author. Note 2: placement of perplexing names on rejected list only by Judicial Commission because decisions affect many well-known names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 58 – refer doubtful spellings to Judicial Commission
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is doubt about different spellings of the same name or epithet, or where two spellings are sufficiently alike to be confused, the question should be referred to the Judicial Commission, which may issue an Opinion as seems fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Commission prefers one spelling, that spelling should be used by succeeding authors. Example: 'megaterium' over 'megatherium'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 59 – capitalization of epithets from personal names
rubrics_metrics.description: An epithet, even one derived from the name of a person, should not be written with an initial capital letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Shigella flexneri (named after Flexner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 60 – preserve intentional latinizations of personal names
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentional latinizations involving changes in orthography of personal names, particularly earlier authors, must be preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Chauveau latinized as Chauvoe, giving Clostridium chauvoei derived from Chauvoe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 61 – original spelling retained except typographic/orthographic errors
rubrics_metrics.description: The original spelling of a name or epithet must be retained, except typographic or orthographic errors. An unintentional typographical or orthographic error later corrected by the author is to be accepted in its corrected form without affecting status and date of valid publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections can be made by subsequent authors; 'corrig.' may be appended if desired. Note: corrections should be used with reserve especially if change affects first syllable/letter; no grammatical/orthographic corrections accepted for names on Approved Lists, Validation Lists, Notification Lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 62a – transliteration differences treated as orthographic variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Words differing only in transliteration into Latin from other languages not using Latin alphabet are to be treated as orthographic variants unless they are names of taxa based upon different types, in which case they are homonyms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Haemophilus and Hemophilus; see Appendix 9 for account of possible variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 62b – author’s choice when orthographic variants based on same type
rubrics_metrics.description: When there are orthographic variants based on the same type, and there is no clear indication that one is correct, then an author has the right of choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 63 – genitive vs adjectival personal name forms treated as different epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: The genitive and adjectival forms of a personal name are treated as different epithets and not as orthographic variants unless so similar as to cause confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: pasteurii (genitive noun) and pasteurianum (adjective) are treated as different epithets; see Appendix 9 for latinization rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 64 – diacritic signs not used; specific transcriptions prescribed
rubrics_metrics.description: Diacritic signs are not used in names or epithets in bacteriology. In names/epithets derived from words with such signs, signs must be suppressed and letters transcribed: (1) ä, ö, ü → ae, oe, ue; (2) é, è, ê → e; (3) ø, æ, å → oe, ae, aa respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these transcriptions when latinizing names containing diacritics.
